title: Chapter 210 – What the White Bell Holds
html:
[Terrace Four – Hua]

Hua has been the Warden's voice for eleven days, and she has learned that carrying another person's thought is a little like carrying water in cupped hands across a rocking boat. You can do it. You can do it for a long time. But the water is never yours, and the boat never stops, and by the end your palms ache with the effort of not letting go.

She sits cross-legged in the dust of the Quay, a pace behind Mo Yan, and holds the channel open.

The woman in the arch has not moved since the child offered her the bell. The white bell lies in the cracked flesh of her palm, pulsing with the light of a very first morning. Beside it, the black bell lies in Mo Yan's small hand, dull as a river stone. Between them there are ten paces of gray dust, a silence you could lean on, and a question neither of them is willing to ask aloud.

Hua, thinks Veyra Thann. I would like to speak to the girl alone.

She cannot hear you without me.

Then I would like to speak to the girl with only you present. The cool voice has changed. It is lower, with something raw under the exactness, like a knife that has been used to cut bread. Send the others away. The Cartographer may stay. He knows.

Hua turns her head. Jian is standing at the lip of the Quay, one hand on a stone Keeper's shoulder, and he has understood without being told. He gives her the smallest of nods. He touches Lan Xiu's arm, and the two of them withdraw toward the shed, the living girl leaning on him with her half-stone legs dragging, the soundless dust parting around their feet.

Hua lets out a breath she has been holding since sunrise.

Thank you, says Veyra.

---

They go into the arch itself, the three of them: the hooded woman, the child, and Hua, who walks behind with her palm burning. The Cartographer follows at a distance, a heavy, slow-moving shape, and stops at the pillar to rub his eyes.

Beneath the arch it is cooler. The stone is carved, and in the dim light Hua sees that the carvings are not decorative. They are a list. Names, in rows, in a script so small and regular it could have been cut by a machine. Four hundred of them, and beside each name a tiny character she recognizes from the Hall of Ten Thousand Names: the mark for Keeper, sleeping.

At the very end of the last row, where the stone is newer, there is a single name with no mark beside it, as though the carver ran out of room, or courage.

Sera, it reads.

Veyra Thann sits down on the stone bench against the wall.

She does it with the stiffness of someone unaccustomed to bending. The long gray cloak gathers around her. She does not push back the hood, but she lowers her bandaged hand, with the white bell pulsing in the palm, to rest in her lap, and for a moment she looks, Hua thinks, like what she is: a tired woman who has been awake for eleven days after sleeping for six hundred years.

Sit, she says.

Mo Yan sits. She puts the black bell in her lap, between her knees.

You asked me whether there was anyone I would take back. The voice is steady. I should tell you about the girl first. It will be easier if I begin there.

Hua says nothing. The channel is a thread of cold fire between them, and she keeps it taut.

---

My daughter's name is Sera, says Veyra Thann. She was nine when she went into the bell.

Nine, thinks Mo Yan.

Yes. Like the Ferryman's. Like you. A pause. It is not an accident. The Founders chose nine because a child of nine has had time to be loved and has not yet had time to be afraid of anything very much. They found, in the first days of the Seam, that the Bloom could be pushed back by a voice, but only a voice that was not afraid. They tried adults. The adults died. They tried the old. The old shattered. They tried children.

Hua's throat tightens.

They did not ask, says the voice. That is the thing I want you to understand. They did not ask any of us. They asked the Keepers, who were already sworn, and the Keepers sent their children, because a Keeper's child is raised to believe the Terrace is a mother. I knew what would be asked. I knew a month before. I could have taken her and run. I did not. The hand in her lap tightens, and the white bell flares. I told myself it was duty. I told myself the Seam was bigger than one child. I put her in the Fourth Terrace myself, in the cradle the Cartographer had drawn, and I held her hand while the Founders spoke the words.

And she sang, whispers Mo Yan.

She sang. For three years. The voice cracks, once, like ice. And then she stopped. And the Bloom went through her, and out the other side. And what was left was the white bell, and the Stair-Father's apology.

The Cartographer, at the pillar, has put his face in his bandaged hand.

That was the end of my marriage, says Veyra. I mean that literally. He was the Stair-Father, then. He is now. His name was Orrin Thann, and he was my husband, and he stood at the Seam and told me Sera had given her life for the world. Her head lifts slightly. I told him that she had not given it. That it had been taken. He did not argue. That was the worst of it. He agreed.

---

Hua's head is ringing.

She did not know, until now, that the Tenth was a man with a surname. She did not know he had been married. The shadow that wore her mark and probed the ward at Terrace Two had spoken in the Tenth's cadence, the grave, patient, dead-voiced courtesy of a priest at a funeral, and it had not occurred to her that the man behind the courtesy could have lain awake at night, listening for a child's voice.

Then he is not a god, she thinks.

He is not a god. Veyra's mouth, under the hood, makes a sound that might once have been a laugh. He is a man who made a bargain in a hurry, and kept it for six hundred years. I do not say he is blameless. I say he is more like Ye Shuhan than like the thing Ye Shuhan believes in.

And the Seam?

The Seam is what it was always. A tear. A place where the world is thin. The Founders found it, and they could not mend it, and they held it with what they had. The cool voice steadies. They held it with children. Then they held it with Keepers. Then they held it with a man who volunteered, who was foolish enough to think he could hold it alone, and was sworn in by his own wife.

Hua's stomach turns.

You, she thinks.

I swore him in, says Veyra Thann. I turned the key on the Tenth Door and sealed him at the top. It was the last thing I did before I went to sleep. She lifts her bare hand with the ring of ember. That is why I carry the second key. I was not its holder by gift. I was its holder because I was the one who locked him in.

Mo Yan is crying silently, and she does not seem to know it.

And now he has turned his own key, Veyra says, and woken me, and asked me to come up. And I have come down. The hooded head turns toward Hua. You have been asking yourself why. I am going to tell you.

---

He is not tired, says Veyra Thann. That is the lie.

Hua feels the channel flinch.

He told the shadow to say he was tired. He told the Cartographer to say he wanted a successor. He has been telling it, in many mouths, to anyone who might listen. And it is true, in the way that the surface of a lake is true. But under it—

She stops.

Hua waits.

A man who has held a door against the Bloom for six hundred years does not grow tired, says Veyra. He grows careful. He grows still. He grows used to the weight. What he does not do is write letters. The bare hand opens, closes. The first key was not a summons. It was a signal. When I felt it turn, in my stone bed, I thought: he is asking for help. And then I thought: Orrin Thann has never asked for help in his life. He would sooner be cut in half.

So it is a trap, Hua thinks.

Or a plea. The voice is very quiet. Or something that uses his hand to be both.

The Cartographer takes his face out of his palm. In the dim light under the arch his eyes are red.

She told me this on the first night, he says, in his gentle, creaking voice. She said she thought the key was not his. I did not want to believe her. He rubs the heel of his hand across his cheek. I have known Orrin a long time. I have drawn his hand. I have seen it shake when he thinks no one is looking. I thought—I thought a husband could not do that.

Do what? Mo Yan asks.

Speak with a voice that is not his own, says Veyra Thann.

And she lifts the white bell from her lap and holds it out.

---

Take it, she says. Do not be afraid.

Hua's breath stops. I cannot. I am not the one who—

It is not you who must take it. It is the child. The hooded head turns. You have paid, little one. You have been where she is. I would ask you to hold it, and tell me what you hear.

Mo Yan looks at Hua. Hua nods, because she does not trust her voice, even a thought-voice, and the child sets the dead black bell down on the stone bench and holds out both hands.

The white bell is placed in them.

For a long moment, nothing happens. Mo Yan cups the little stone in her palms, and the cracked line of dark glows faintly, and a thin steady light leaks between her fingers. Then her shoulders drop. Her eyes close. Her whole small body goes very still, in the particular way of a child who is listening to something far away.

She's singing, Mo Yan whispers.

Hua goes cold.

It's not a song. It's just— The child's brow wrinkles. It's one note. It goes on and on. It's not loud. It's like someone humming in another room, and they don't know you can hear. Her lips part. She sounds so tired.

Sera, says Veyra Thann, and the name falls from her like a stone dropped down a well.

She doesn't hear me, Mo Yan says. She's—she's not here. She's far. I think she's— Her face changes. Oh.

What is it?

She's not alone.

The Cartographer takes a step forward.

There's someone with her, Mo Yan says. Her voice is small and precise, the voice of a child reading a difficult word from a page. Someone is with her, and they're not singing. They're answering. Every time she hums, they answer. And the answer is— She opens her eyes, and they are black and stunned. It's the Seam. It's the Bloom. It's answering her in her own voice.

What does it say? Veyra whispers.

Mo Yan swallows. It says, "Come up, Mother."

---

For a long time, no one speaks.

The arch is very cold. The names on the stone seem to lean close. Hua can hear, through the channel, the faint wild flutter of a heart: Veyra's, stopping and starting, the heartbeat of a woman who has been told that the thing she has run from for six hundred years has her daughter's voice.

Not Orrin, Veyra breathes. Not Orrin who wrote it.

It was the Bloom, says the Cartographer, very quietly. It used his hand to turn the key. It knew you would come.

It wanted me awake. Veyra's voice has gone flat and small. It wanted me to go up.

Yes.

And I came down instead. A sound comes out of the hood that is half a sob and half a laugh. I was so afraid. I thought I was being clever. I thought if I closed the road, it would be shut out. And all the while it was waiting for me to run, because if I ran, it would never have to ask again.

Mo Yan, with the white bell in her hands, has gone very still.

Veyra, she says, with the careful gentleness of a child handing a hot cup to an elder. If you close the road, Sera is on the other side. With it. Forever.

Yes.

And if you go up—

It will have me. The cool voice says it quite simply. I think it will. I think that is what it has wanted all along. A holder of the second key, awake, willing, in front of the door. A breath. And Orrin will be there. And he will be as he is. And I do not know what I am afraid of more.

Hua's hand has closed on the mark in her palm. It is burning, steadily, like a coal pressed against bone. She understands, with a sudden cold clarity, what Veyra has been doing for two days. She has not been deciding whether to close the road. She has been deciding whether she is brave enough to open it.

I will go, says Hua.

It slips out. She had not meant to say it.

I will go up. I carry the third piece of the key. I am the Warden's voice. If someone must stand in front of the door, it should not be you alone. She swallows. And I would rather it was someone who is not afraid.

You are afraid, says Veyra.

Very.

Good. The hooded head turns toward her, and for the first time Hua sees, in the shadow of the hood, the line of a cheek, the corner of a mouth. It is a face that has been beautiful, and tired for a very long time. Then you have paid.

---

---

Veyra gives them the rule before they leave the arch.

She does it standing, in the doorway, with the white bell wrapped again in its gray cloth and her hood turned toward the first stars. She speaks to Hua alone, because Hua is the one who holds the channel, and because, Hua suspects, it is easier for her to speak to someone who cannot see her face.

There is one thing the Founders learned about the Bloom, she says. They learned it late, and at great cost. It cannot make a voice. It can only borrow one.

Borrow?

It answers in the voice of whoever is listening for. If you are afraid, it is the voice of what you fear. If you are lonely, it is the voice of what you lost. The hood does not turn. It cannot lie, in the strict sense. Everything it says, the person it has taken once said, or would have said. It finds the words in the dark of the swallowed mind, and it wears them.

Then Sera did say it.

Sera said it, once, in another place, in another year, to me. The voice is very flat. "Come up, Mother." She called me that from the top of a staircase when she was five, because I was late for supper and she wanted me to see something. It is not a threat. It is a memory with the sharp end turned toward me. A pause. That is how it works. It does not need to invent a cruelty. It only needs to find the kindest thing you ever heard, and say it at the wrong time.

Hua's mouth is dry. How do you resist it?

You do not. The first dry hint of humor. You hear it. You let it be as true as it is. And then you remember who is speaking.

How?

By the cost. Veyra lifts her bandaged hand a little. A real voice costs the speaker something. Sera's cost her three years. The Ferryman's cost him his life. Yours costs you a day each time you open the channel, and you have never once complained. She turns, at last. The line of her mouth is steady. The Bloom speaks for free. That is how you know. When a voice that loves you asks you for something, and asks for nothing in return, and offers every comfort, and does not tire, it is not the one you loved.

Hua says nothing. She is thinking of the shadow at Terrace Two, wearing the real mark with such easy confidence. It had never paid. It had never even seemed to care what it spent.

You will remember that, says Veyra.

I will.

Good. The hood lowers. Then you are the second person I have trusted in six hundred years.

Who was the first?

The man I locked in the tower, says Veyra Thann, and goes out into the dust.

---

Hua finds Lan Xiu on the Quay an hour later, sitting among the stone pupils with her blanket around her shoulders and her legs stretched out in front of her. The living girl has not gone to bed. She is writing.

She has covered an entire slab of the Quay in her neat scholar's hand, and Hua, stopping at her shoulder, sees that it is a list. Five names, a line each. After each name, a few small notes: a favorite food, a joke they used to tell, the name of a mother in a village Hua has never heard of.

So that I remember, writes Lan Xiu, when she notices her. If I forget. The Cartographer says the bell takes things.

It did not take yours.

It might. The finger hesitates. I woke up. That is a kind of paying. I do not know what mine will be.

Hua sits down in the dust beside her.

She has been avoiding this conversation since the child came out of the dark with a soft face and a hole where her mother used to be. She has not wanted to look at what the road costs. She has been doing the arithmetic in quiet corners: eleven days of the channel, eleven days of her life, a few weeks thinner than she was at the Wall. It is not much. It is more than she will say.

I would like to ask you something, she says. You were awake when Veyra Thann put the others to stone.

I was not awake. I was frozen. But I could hear.

What did she say?

Lan Xiu's finger moves slowly.

She said "Forgive me." She said it five times, once for each of us, and once more, to the one at the end, who was me. She said it to every face. The finger stops. She did not say it to Elder Ye. She said it to us.

Hua closes her eyes.

She is coming with us, she writes, in the dust, beneath the list. She means to undo it, if she can.

Lan Xiu reads it three times.

Then I will wait, she writes at last. I am good at waiting. I have had practice. And, below that, in smaller letters, her mouth curving in a smile that does not reach her eyes: Tell her I forgive her. Not for her sake. For mine. It is very heavy to hold onto.

Hua nods.

She sits with the girl until the stars come out, and the list on the stone is finished, and the five stone faces stand around them in the cold blue dark with their mouths open on five different words.

Hua goes back to the shed late, when the stars are out.

Jian is waiting by the stove, which the Cartographer has finally lit, and he stands when she comes in. He takes in her face. He does not ask. He waits, with the patience he has learned in these weeks, and Hua understands that he has been standing for an hour with his shaking hand tucked in his sleeve, rehearsing a dozen ways to say the thing he is about to say.

"She is coming," Hua tells him. "She will not close the road."

He lets out a breath.

"She will come up with us, as far as the Seventh Terrace. After that—" Hua spreads her hands. "She does not know. Neither do I."

"And the Bridge?"

"I told her."

Jian goes still.

"I told her what it costs," Hua says. "Not you. Me. The Cartographer had it on the map, in the margin, in a hand I could read. A day of her spine, for every Terrace." She holds his eyes. "She laughed. She said she had known for six hundred years. It was the first thing the Founders told her about the key. She did not tell you because you did not ask."

"I did not know to ask."

"No." Hua smiles faintly. It is the first time in days. "It seems we have all been protecting each other from the same secret."

Jian sits down on the bench. For a moment he puts his face in his good hand, and she thinks he might laugh. When he lifts his head, his eyes are bright.

"Then we use the Bridge," he says.

"She will not let you carry the cost alone. She wants it known. She said, in her words, that she would sooner pay with her spine than her conscience."

"Seven Terraces," Jian says slowly. "Seven days of a person's spine."

"She has them to give."

"She has more to lose than that."

"Yes." Hua looks at the stove, where the Cartographer is feeding the fire with flat white slivers of his maps, one by one. "That is why she is coming."

On the bench by the wall, Mo Yan has fallen asleep with the white bell still in her palms. Lan Xiu has wrapped a blanket around her. The light from the crack in the stone makes a thin, steady line across the child's face.

Jian looks at it for a long time.

"Hua," he says. "What is the Seam answering with?"

She tells him.

She tells him about the voice that says Come up, Mother, and the humming in the other room, and the girl who has been singing for six hundred years because nobody told her she could stop. She tells him about the Tenth's hand that shakes. She tells him about the key that was not a plea, and the bargain made in a hurry.

When she finishes, Jian is silent.

Then he says, in a voice she has never heard from him, a voice stripped of every layer he has built:

"It is learning to use them."

"The Bloom?"

"The people it has taken. Sera. Orrin's hand. The shadow." He looks up. "It does not need a body. It needs a voice somebody loves."

The stove ticks. The Cartographer's maps burn, one by one, in a small, steady fire. Outside the shed the night gathers over the Silent Terrace, and the four hundred sleeping Keepers, and the five stone pupils on the Quay, and the great arch with its list of names.

"And somewhere above us," Jian says, "it has Wenyuan's brother's voice, and Qinghe's mother's, and every child's it has ever swallowed. Waiting for the day one of us climbs high enough to answer."

Hua does not reply. There is nothing to say.

On the bench, in her sleep, Mo Yan turns her head toward the white bell, and her lips shape, without sound, a name she does not remember losing.

Sera, she mouths.

And from the bell in her hands, very faintly, so faintly that only Hua, with the mark burning in her palm, hears it, a thin tired voice, nine years old and six hundred years worn, answers:

Is that you, Mama?
